svg.text: A 30,000-app workspace: what a change actually costs
30,000 Next.js apps + 460 shared libs in one workspace — about 1.03 million generated files. Every number below was measured on this tree.
1. How far does a change reach?
5 of the libs are imported by every app. Change one and the pipeline re-runs a task for every package (plus the lib builds); change an ordinary lib
and almost nothing runs.
30,708 tasks re-run
edit a lib that EVERY app imports (the worst case)
100 tasks re-run
edit an ordinary leaf lib — 307× smaller blast radius
2. The worst case, run two ways (64-core box)
Same question — “did my change break any app?” — two mechanisms. Not like-for-like: the pipeline also builds each lib's dist output; the one command
only type-checks.
60.7s — one command
a single checker reads the whole workspace's source once
(peak memory: 51,321MB recorded — a ~50GB-class box)
10.2 min — ×10.1 slower
standard pipeline: 30,708 tasks — a checker process
per affected package plus 460 lib builds
A breaking change is caught in 59.5s
all 30,000 affected apps flagged with exact file and line — the fix-list a codemod can consume
3. Does a bigger machine help?
The same two mechanisms on two different machines (64 vs 192 cores, recorded per run). One comparison each — a cross-machine observation, not a
controlled core-scaling experiment.
one command, 64 cores: 60.7s
one process; the smaller box was faster
one command, 192 cores: 65.8s
×1.1 slower — this check did not gain from the bigger box
pipeline, 64 cores: 10.2 min
×1.6 slower than the big box
pipeline, 192 cores: 6.5 min
ran 1.6× faster on this box (3.0× the cores)
also measured: installing the 30,460-package workspace (plus its external deps) takes 181s (bun, warm store) · linting the whole tree takes 2.9s (oxlint)
toolchain: bun 1.3.14 · turbo 2.9.18 · tsgo 7.0.0-dev.20260707.2
